title: Guduchi / Giloy (Tinospora cordifolia): Uses, Evidence & Safety
metaDescription: Guduchi or giloy (Tinospora cordifolia): traditional Ayurvedic use as an immune tonic, what the science shows, and the documented liver-injury cautions.
h1: Guduchi (Tinospora cordifolia): Traditional Use, Evidence and Cautions
answerCapsule: Guduchi (Tinospora cordifolia), also called giloy, is a climbing shrub used in Ayurveda as a rasayana and immune tonic. Modern laboratory work has studied its immunomodulatory compounds [1]. Human evidence remains limited. Published Indian case series have linked giloy supplements to autoimmune-like liver injury [2][3], so quality, supervision and honest caution matter more than the marketing around it.

sections.capsule: Guduchi (Sanskrit गुडूची, IAST guḍūcī; botanical name Tinospora cordifolia) is a heart-leaved climbing vine native to the Indian subcontinent, widely sold today as giloy. Classical Ayurvedic texts class it as a rasayana and amrita — the nectar herb — valued as a bitter digestive and immune tonic. The stem is the part most often used, as juice, powder or extract.
sections.body:
Guduchi belongs to the Menispermaceae family and grows across India, often twining over neem and mango trees. Its Sanskrit names carry its reputation: *guḍūcī* (that which guards the body) and *amṛtā* (the imperishable, or nectar of immortality), a naming that tells you how highly the tradition regarded it.

In classical terms it is described as *tikta* (bitter) and *kaṣāya* (astringent) in taste, light and warming, and is grouped among the *rasayana* herbs — those used for rejuvenation and vitality [1]. It is traditionally taken to kindle digestion (*agni*) and as a general tonic where [pitta or vata](/doshas) is aggravated. The stem — as *satva*, a starch extract, or as a simple decoction — is used more than the leaf. Reputable products name *Tinospora cordifolia* on the label, because a closely related species, *Tinospora crispa*, carries its own separate safety concerns.

sections.h2: What does the science say about guduchi?
sections.capsule: Guduchi has been studied mainly in laboratory and animal models, where its compounds show immunomodulatory and antioxidant activity [1]. Robust human trials are scarce, and the herb is studied rather than proven for any use. The most important recent evidence is a safety signal: a 2022 nationwide Indian study documented 43 people who developed liver injury after taking giloy [3].
sections.body:
Guduchi is one of the most heavily marketed Ayurvedic herbs, promoted during the COVID-19 pandemic and dengue seasons as an immune booster. The honest position is that most of this reputation rests on cell and animal research — studies describing immunomodulatory, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity of its alkaloids and polysaccharides [1]. Well-designed human trials that would confirm a clinical benefit are few and small, so giloy is best seen as *studied for* immune support, not established for it.

What emerged clearly from recent research was a warning rather than a benefit. During the pandemic, clinicians across India reported a cluster of patients who developed acute liver injury with autoimmune features after self-medicating with giloy. A case series described six such patients [2], and a multicentre study across thirteen centres identified 43 [3]. See [Is Ayurveda scientific?](/is-ayurveda-scientific) for how signals like this fit the wider evidence picture.

sections.h2: What are the side effects and cautions of guduchi?
sections.capsule: Guduchi is usually well tolerated in short traditional use, but the documented concern is liver injury: Indian case reports and a 43-patient study describe autoimmune-like hepatitis after prolonged or unsupervised giloy use [2][3]. Guduchi may lower blood sugar, so care is needed with diabetes medicines. Avoid it in pregnancy and with autoimmune liver disease. Stop and seek medical advice for jaundice or dark urine.
sections.body:
The cautions that matter, in order of importance:

- **Liver injury:** the clearest documented risk. Reports from India describe people developing acute hepatitis with autoimmune features after weeks of giloy, some with pre-existing silent autoimmune liver disease that the herb appears to unmask [2][3]. Warning signs include yellowing of the eyes or skin, dark urine, nausea and unusual fatigue — stop the herb and see a doctor promptly.
- **Correct identification:** *Tinospora cordifolia* must not be confused with *Tinospora crispa*, which has separately reported liver toxicity. Botanical accuracy on the label matters.
- **Blood sugar:** guduchi may lower blood glucose, so monitor closely if you take diabetes medication, and watch for additive effects.
- **Autoimmune conditions:** because it stimulates immune activity, it is best avoided if you have an autoimmune disease, and used only under supervision.
- **Pregnancy and breastfeeding:** safety is not established; avoid.
- **Contamination:** as with any herbal product, heavy-metal contamination is a sourcing risk, not a property of the plant [4]. Choose a maker that follows a recognised Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standard with heavy-metal testing.

Prolonged, high-dose or unsupervised use is the pattern common to the reported liver cases, which is exactly why casual long-term self-dosing is unwise.

sections.h2: Where can I find quality guduchi?
sections.capsule: Guduchi's real risks come from prolonged unsupervised use and from poor sourcing rather than from the plant itself, so quality control is central. Prefer products that name Tinospora cordifolia, are made to a recognised Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standard, and are tested for heavy metals [4]. Where guduchi is used within care, it is prescribed and monitored by a physician at an NABH-accredited Ayurvedic hospital.
sections.body:
Guduchi sold under a recognised **Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standard**, with confirmed botanical identity and heavy-metal testing, is the practical answer to the two things that have caused harm: mis-identified plant material and contaminated supplements [4]. That is a statement about quality control, not a claim that guduchi treats any medical condition.

Given the documented liver signal, guduchi is a herb to approach through a qualified Ayurvedic physician rather than casual self-dosing — someone who can weigh it against your history, medicines and liver health. Compare it with the other herbs in this cluster, such as [ashwagandha](/herbs/ashwagandha), [triphala](/herbs/triphala) and [shilajit](/herbs/shilajit), and see the [herbs hub](/herbs) for how sourcing quality is assessed.

faqs.q: Is giloy safe for the liver?
faqs.a: Giloy has been linked to rare but serious liver injury in published Indian reports, including a study of 43 patients who developed autoimmune-like hepatitis after taking it [3]. Most recovered after stopping. It is not a herb to take long-term without supervision, and anyone with liver disease should avoid it.

faqs.q: What is guduchi or giloy used for in Ayurveda?
faqs.a: In Ayurveda, guduchi (giloy) is classified as a rasayana and is traditionally taken as a bitter digestive and immune tonic, and to support recovery and vitality. These are traditional uses described in classical texts, not proven medical treatments, and modern human evidence for specific benefits remains limited.

faqs.q: Can I take giloy for immunity or COVID?
faqs.a: Giloy was widely promoted as an immunity booster during COVID-19, but that popularity outran the evidence, and the same period produced reports of giloy-associated liver injury [2]. There is no reliable clinical evidence that it wards off or shortens infections, so it should not replace vaccination or medical care.

faqs.q: How is giloy taken — juice, powder or tablet?
faqs.a: Traditionally the stem of guduchi is used as a fresh juice, a starch extract called guduchi satva, a powder, or a decoction; modern products also sell it as capsules and tablets. Because dose and duration matter for safety, and long unsupervised courses feature in the liver-injury reports, it is best used on a physician's guidance.
